name: Sass
one_liner: CSS preprocessor adding variables, nesting and mixins, compiled to plain CSS.
what_it_is: A CSS preprocessor adding variables, nesting, mixins, functions and modules, compiled to plain CSS. The SCSS syntax is, with a few small exceptions, a superset of CSS — essentially all valid CSS is valid SCSS, in the project’s own words.
why_it_matters: Sass is still in wide production use and remains a perfectly reasonable choice — but the ground shifted underneath it. Native custom properties, native nesting and modern layout removed the reasons most people originally reached for it, and its own @import was deprecated in favour of @use. What still has no native equivalent is mixins and compile-time logic. If Sass is where your styling knowledge stopped, the useful question is not whether to abandon it, but which of its features you are still running a build step for when the browser now does them natively.
suitable_for: Existing codebases with substantial Sass already written
Design systems that genuinely need mixins and compile-time logic
Teams wanting partials and file organisation without a bundler-driven approach
not_suitable_for: New projects wanting only variables and nesting, which CSS now provides natively
Projects trying to remove build steps from their styling pipeline
Teams who would be better served by a shared token scale than by a preprocessor
